lines.text: Reaction names become useful when they tell you exactly what changes in bonds or electrons. The same short vocabulary works across the organic syllabus.

A homologous series has the same functional group and general formula, successive members differ by C H two. Saturated compounds have only carbon carbon single bonds, unsaturated compounds have a carbon carbon multiple bond. Homolytic fission gives one bonding electron to each atom, forming free radicals with unpaired electrons. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one atom, forming ions. Radical initiation generates radicals, propagation consumes and regenerates radicals, and termination removes radicals by combination. A nucleophile donates an electron pair, an electrophile accepts one. Addition combines reactants into one product, substitution replaces an atom or group, elimination removes atoms or groups, often forming a multiple bond. Hydrolysis breaks a bond using water, condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule. Organic oxidation is gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, and reduction is loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. open square bracket O close square bracket and open square bracket H close square bracket represent one atom of oxygen from an oxidising agent and one atom of hydrogen from a reducing agent, respectively.
Electron pair donors are nucleophiles, electron pair acceptors are electrophiles. This links the reaction labels here to the four mechanism types in the next idea.

Homolysis gives radicals, heterolysis gives ions. Initiation creates, propagation sustains, termination removes radicals. Addition joins, substitution replaces, elimination removes. Hydrolysis uses water, condensation loses a small molecule. Oxidation gains O or loses H, reduction loses O or gains H.
Why can a neutral molecule be a nucleophile, and how would you distinguish homolytic from heterolytic fission in an electron diagram?

Which description identifies homolytic fission? Both bonding electrons move to one atom. Each bonded atom receives one electron. An electron pair moves from a lone pair to carbon. A bond breaks by reaction with water. B Equal division of the bonding pair forms two radicals.
A mechanism explains a reaction at electron level. Its name predicts both the attacking species and the overall bond change.

Free radical substitution replaces an atom through radical initiation, propagation and termination, alkane chlorination under U V light is an example. Electrophilic addition begins when an alkene pi bond donates a pair to an electrophile, addition across C double bond C follows. Nucleophilic substitution begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to a carbon attached to a leaving group, which departs, cyanide replacing bromide is an example. Nucleophilic addition begins when a nucleophile donates a lone pair to the partially positive carbonyl carbon, the C double bond O pair moves to oxygen, and the alkoxide can then be protonated. Full curly arrows represent movement of electron pairs, so each arrow must start at the source bond or lone pair and point to the destination. Show relevant bond polarity and charges. A radical step instead transfers single electrons and uses single headed arrows when drawn.

thirteen point two Characteristic organic reactions.
In one breath.

Classify an organic reaction by what changes in the molecules, then classify its mechanism by how electrons move. A full curly arrow follows an electron pair from a bond or lone pair to its destination.
Key ideas.

A homologous series is a family with the same functional group and general formula, successive members differ by C H two. A saturated organic compound contains only carbon carbon single bonds. An unsaturated compound contains a carbon carbon double or triple bond.

In homolytic fission, each bonded atom receives one electron, forming free radicals, species with an unpaired electron. In heterolytic fission, one atom receives both bonding electrons, forming ions. During a radical chain reaction, initiation forms radicals, propagation uses a radical and produces another, and termination combines radicals to remove them.

A nucleophile donates an electron pair, an electrophile accepts one. These may be ions or neutral molecules. Addition joins reactants to give one product, often across a multiple bond. Substitution replaces an atom or group. Elimination removes atoms or groups, often forming a multiple bond. Hydrolysis breaks a bond by reaction with water. Condensation joins molecules with loss of a small molecule, commonly water.

Figure, Hydroxide lone pair attacks a proton, follow the curly arrow from oxygen to hydrogen, source, nine seven zero one c13.2, p.18. Notice that the red curly arrow starts at the oxygen lone pair and points to the hydrogen ion, showing where that electron pair forms a new bond.

In organic chemistry, oxidation can mean gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen, reduction can mean loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen. In equations, open square bracket O close square bracket represents one oxygen atom supplied by an oxidising agent, open square bracket H close square bracket represents one hydrogen atom supplied by a reducing agent.
Method.
Identify what enters, leaves or changes, this gives addition, substitution, elimination, hydrolysis, condensation or redox.
Track the attacking species. A nucleophile donates a lone pair to an electron poor centre, an electrophile accepts a pair from an electron rich bond or lone pair.
For a full curly arrow, begin at the bond or lone pair supplying two electrons and end where the pair goes. Show relevant bond polarity and charges.

H C L alkene arrow check, Start the first full curly arrow at the middle of the C double bond C pi bond and point it to H in H C L. At the same time, draw a second full curly arrow from the H C L bond to chlorine, that bond pair moves to chlorine. Do not start the first arrow at H C L or at a bonded carbon atom, its tail must identify the alkene electron pair.
Worked example.

Classify the reaction of a ketone with H C N and describe the key arrows. The C double bond O bond is polar, carbon is delta plus and oxygen delta minus. The carbon end of C N minus supplies a lone pair to the carbonyl carbon. At the same time, the C double bond O electron pair moves to oxygen. The resulting alkoxide is protonated to give a hydroxynitrile. This is nucleophilic addition because cyanide adds across the carbonyl group.

The four mechanism names combine the attacker and the overall change. Free radical substitution replaces an atom through a radical chain, as in alkane chlorination under U V light. Electrophilic addition adds an electrophile across an alkene C double bond C bond, its pi electrons first attack the electrophile. Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group, as when C N minus replaces bromide in a halogenoalkane. Nucleophilic addition adds a nucleophile across a carbonyl C double bond O bond.
Traps.
Trap, Treating homolysis as ion formation. Why it's wrong, each atom takes one bonding electron. Instead, draw radicals with unpaired electrons.
Trap, Starting a curly arrow at the atom being attacked. Why it's wrong, that atom is the destination, not the electron source. Instead, start at a bond or lone pair.
Trap, Assuming every nucleophile is negatively charged. Why it's wrong, neutral molecules such as ammonia donate lone pairs. Instead, test for an available electron pair.
Exam technique.

For Define, give the electron pair wording precisely. For Describe a mechanism, include charges or polarity and place each arrow's tail at the electron pair, in nucleophilic addition, do not invent a positive carbonyl intermediate. Use open square bracket O close square bracket and open square bracket H close square bracket only with their stated one atom meanings.
